extracted.intended_audience: architects, architecture students, and designers concerned with stone construction and classical/gothic pier/shaft design
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and aesthetic guidelines for designing pier bases, spurs, and shafts in stone construction: material choice, proportions, execution limits, grouping, and the relationship between structural truth and visual expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish visual impression from structural reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not confuse the eye's feeling of firmness with real structural stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes to a base may slightly increase real security but are often made chiefly to convince the eye of security. Always assess whether an element is actually performing a structural role or merely giving the appearance of support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spurs/props as expressive not structural elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Spurs or props are often structurally useless yet highly important as an expression of safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their triangular/animal-claw-like form is chosen because it best expresses support; width could be arbitrary but the visual form matters. They may be made wider in reality, but shown narrow in diagrams for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrate substance where loads concentrate (use single stones)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the whole weight of the building rests on few limited spaces, those members should, if possible, be of solid masonry or single stones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Xb and Yb should each be a single stone or both cut from one block, especially if spurs are added. A single block provides a surface free from joints and is perceived by the eye as a firm covering over the smaller masonry beneath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yb height-to-width proportion limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Limits on the height of the base member Yb relative to its width.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Yb looks so thin that the column above might break it, it is too low; if higher than its own width it is too high. The utmost admissible height is that of a cubic block (height ≤ width).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of plan expansion for base (square best generally)
rubrics_metrics.description: Yb may expand into square, pentagon, hexagon, or other polygons but the square is usually best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As the number of sides increases, spurs become shorter and less energetic; therefore the square often gives the best expressive and structural effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedestals as permanent devices
rubrics_metrics.description: A pedestal is a make-shift, not an additional perfection, and should be used only when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pedestals only to raise shafts to match neighbouring levels or to set delicate materials at the proper height; do not adopt pedestals as ornamental permanent substitutes for true bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal shaft: block shaft of single stone
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfect shaft is a single stone hewn into an elongated cylindrical (slightly convex) form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Block shafts should be composed of stone free from flaws or fissures (crystalline rocks like marble). Where obtainable, prefer block shafts for their material quality and symmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shaft profile: slight convex taper, not straight cone or bulge
rubrics_metrics.description: Shafts should be slightly thicker at the base and taper slightly to the top in a very slight convex curve, not bulging at the centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A straight-sided cone is difficult and risky to cut; leave a little extra and work the shaft slightly convex, smoothing the curve by eye. The curve should taper faster toward the top than near the ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material suitability governs style and feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The geological nature of building stone determines whether block shafts are feasible and thus influences architectural style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English thin-bedded rocks rarely allow large block shafts (exceptions: granites, whinstones); abundance of marble/travertine in Greece/Italy enabled classical shaft types. Architects must consider available materials when choosing forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish jointed (stacked) versus filled-up (masonry) shafts
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two practical alternatives to block shafts: jointed (slices of shaft stacked) and filled-up towers (small stones cemented into a mass).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jointed columns (even if composed of many thin slices) can be nearly as strong as block shafts provided no horizontal dislocating forces act; filled-up towers are more liable to fissure if cement fails and therefore have different limits on form and thickness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curvature often impractical or unsafe in pieced/filled shafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Curved outlines of shafts are difficult to execute on jointed or filled-up shafts and can be structurally unsafe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fitting a curve across many joints requires great care; in filled-up towers the shell provides strength and would burst if curved outwards under heavy load. Curvature in such shafts, if retained, is for aesthetic reasons only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jointed/cemented shafts require larger bulk
rubrics_metrics.description: Shafts composed of many joints or small stones must be thicker for the same load than single-block shafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of increased risk of horizontal dislocation or fissure, jointed and cemented shafts should be bulkier (thicker in proportion to weight carried) than monolithic shafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tapering is harder with many joints; execution drives form
rubrics_metrics.description: With numerous joints or irregular stones tapering is difficult to achieve; builders may default to straight (plumb) shafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When joints are numerous ('pile of cheeses') it is natural to cut all segments to the same diameter or build by plumb-line and abandon tapering; consider constructibility when specifying profile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between many slender vs few massy shafts
rubrics_metrics.description: The number and diameter of shafts carrying a weight is a design choice constrained by human scale and building breadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same load may be carried by many slender shafts or few massy ones; limits arise from the inconvenience of narrow intervals and loss of breadth from large shafts. Commonly choose a mean leaning to grace or grandeur according to expression. Materials availability can push choice toward smaller perfect shafts or larger imperfect ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group shafts only with clear structural cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not multiply shafts without visible reason in the arrangement of the superimposed members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The whole value of grouped piers depends on wise fitting to the load and on all members working together. Avoid unnecessary multiplicity which may look decorative but not structural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan arrangement (square vs oblique) signals school and affects support
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrangement of grouped shafts in plan (square/even vs oblique/cross) is a fundamental organizing principle and affects support behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Square-set groups (even) are characteristic of southern/Greek work; oblique (cross) set is characteristic of northern/Gothic. The relative setting influences load distribution and architectural expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design grouped shafts to act in concert; avoid visible separation
rubrics_metrics.description: In a multiple-shaft group avoid a marked separation between a central shaft and its satellites, and ensure satellites are not merely ornamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If satellites appear separated they either look useless or like caging the central shaft (iron rods wiring a cylinder) — a fatal appearance. Aim for integration so the central and satellite shafts expand/work together under load; if central shaft expands faster it may push out or swallow satellites—plan for proportional behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use strength-to-area approximations when dividing load among shafts
rubrics_metrics.description: When dividing required strength among several shafts, assume strength scales (approximately) with the square of diameter for design estimation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author uses strength ∝ diameter^2 as a sufficient approximation for comparative planning: a shaft s can be divided into multiple equal smaller shafts whose aggregated area/strength carries the load accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive foiling (multifoiled profiles) unless justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Multifoiled (trefoil, quatrefoil, cinquefoil) shaft plans exist but are rarely true grouped shafts and should be used with caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multifoiled shafts often represent decorative canaliculation rather than genuine grouping; Gothic quatrefoils are common, Egyptian multifoiled types occur in the south—use only where structurally and expressively appropriate.
